subject: Biology
title: The Mariana Trench
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Mariana Trench usable.

hook.text: The Mariana Trench is nearly 11 km deep. If Mount Everest were placed inside, its peak would still be underwater.

buildup.text: Challenger Deep, the lowest point, has pressure over 1,000 times that at the surface.

discovery.text: In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh descended in the Trieste. They saw a flatfish at the bottom.

twist.text: Researchers found a plastic bag at the bottom of the trench—human pollution reaches even the deepest point.

climax.text: Amphipods living at these depths have evolved unique pressure-resistant proteins to survive.

punchline.text: The deepest place on Earth. Not empty. Not untouched.

quiz.question: How deep is the Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep?

details.summary: The Mariana Trench is the deepest place on Earth at nearly 11,000 meters below sea level. Challenger Deep at its bottom experiences pressures exceeding 1,000 atmospheres yet supports life including amphipods, xenophyophores, and microbial communities adapted to extreme conditions.
details.whyItMatters: The Mariana Trench represents the extreme limit of the biosphere on Earth. Discovering life there proves that organisms can adapt to almost any physical condition, informing the search for extraterrestrial life and deep-sea resource management.
takeaways: Challenger Deep reaches 10,935 meters, the deepest known point on Earth
Pressure at the bottom exceeds 1,000 atmospheres, crushing most materials
Microplastics and human pollutants have been found even at these depths

faq.question: What lives at the bottom of the Mariana Trench?
faq.answer: Amphipod crustaceans scavenge food that sinks from above. Xenophyophores, giant single-celled organisms, carpet the seafloor. Microbial communities metabolize chemicals in the sediment. A snailfish species holds the record for deepest-living fish at 8,336 meters.

faq.question: How many people have visited the bottom of the Mariana Trench?
faq.answer: Only a handful. Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh first reached Challenger Deep in 1960. James Cameron repeated the feat solo in 2012. Victor Vescovo made the deepest-ever dive in 2019. Fewer people have been to the bottom than have walked on the Moon.
